idiom_name: Boost.PropertyTree ptree with typed get/put over a string-keyed document tree
implementation_notes: Boost.PropertyTree replaces the whole class structure: basic_ptree is a loosely typed, dynamically composed document tree (a string key and, by default, a string value per node), get<T>(path)/put(path, value)/get_optional<T>() are the typed views, and '.'-separated paths walk into children. C++ has no interfaces with default implementations to hang traits on, so the view half becomes accessor wrappers or free functions taking the tree. Where the hierarchy must keep real types instead of string data, hand-roll std::unordered_map<std::string, std::any> and read with std::any_cast - a mismatch throws std::bad_any_cast, the language's stand-in for a failed view cast.
pitfalls: ptree stores everything as a string: get<int> re-parses on every access, formatting and precision are lost, and a malformed value throws ptree_bad_data at read time rather than at write time.
'.'-separated paths are ambiguous when keys contain dots; pass an explicit ptree::path_type with another separator instead of a string path.
A key may be repeated in a ptree (each node holds a sequence of children), so get(path) is not deterministic when duplicates exist - iterate get_child instead.

A key may be repeated in a ptree (each node holds a sequence of children), so a path lookup addresses one matching node and duplicates are easy to misinterpret - use unique keys or iterate get_child when multiplicity is intentional.

variants.name: std::any property map with any_cast accessors
variants.implementation_notes: The direct translation of the classic structure into modern C++: the document is an unordered_map<string, any> (child documents are nested maps or vectors of them) and each view is a small accessor type whose getters call std::any_cast<T>, which throws std::bad_any_cast on a wrong type. Choose it over Boost.PropertyTree when views must keep real types instead of round-tripping through strings, or when Boost must not be a dependency; the price is that nothing is serialisable without an adapter.
pitfalls: std::any requires a copy-constructible type and stores a copy, so large documents, move-only values or references cost allocations - store pointers or use std::variant.
props.at() throws std::out_of_range before any_cast can report a type mismatch, so decide whether missing and mistyped are one failure mode or two.
